title: iPhone Duo already backordered until 2027 as pre-order sales soar
summary: Consumer demand for Apple's first foldable phone is strong despite the device's hefty $1,999 price tag.
story: Apple is seeing strong demand for its new foldable iPhone, with supplies quickly selling out after pre-order sales opened on Friday.

"Apple opened iPhone Duo pre-orders this morning, and the early read looks robust in our view, with demand for Cupertino's first foldable running well ahead of supply out of the gates," Wall Street analyst Dan Ives, a partner at Yorkville Ives, said in a research note.

The pre-order window for the Duo opened on Friday at 8 a.m. ET on apple.com and in the Apple Store app. Within minutes, the estimated delivery of the phone was pushed back past Oct. 23, the device's official launch date, and into next year. As of Friday afternoon, the Apple phone was backordered until late January.
"It's been 3 minutes, and it's sold out at every store around the NYC/CT area," Max Weinbach, an analyst for the market research firm Creativestrat, said on X.
Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how many pre-order requests it received.

Apple's new CEO, John Ternus, announced the iPhone Duo last month. The Duo lets users split the screen to use two different apps on the device, or two windows of the same website for uses such as comparison shopping.

Prices start at $1,999 for a device with 256 GB of storage. When folded, it's about the size of a passport. The full display is the largest of any Apple phone, resembling more of an iPad than an iPhone.
Ternus also announced the iPhone 18 at Apple's annual fall showcase, which went on sale last month.

Ives thinks demand for the Duo will remain strong into 2027, with many iPhone users planning to upgrade. He projects Apple will sell around 10 million Duos in the next few quarters and up to 25 million in 2027.

title: Fighter jets intercept plane over South Carolina during Trump rally
summary: Fighter jets intercepted a plane that entered restricted airspace over Clemson, South Carolina, on Wednesday, as President Trump spoke at a rally there, military officials said.
story: Fighter jets intercepted a plane that was flying through restricted airspace Wednesday over Clemson, South Carolina, military officials said. The incident happened as President Trump held a rally at Clemson University to support Darline  Graham's Senate campaign.

F-16 aircraft were deployed just after 5:30 p.m. ET to intercept a general aviation plane that had violated a temporary flight restriction in that area, according to the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD. Temporary flight restrictions are issued by the FAA for a variety of reasons, ranging from extreme weather to large athletic, entertainment or political events. Such restrictions are often put in place over a town or city when high-profile figures, especially the president, are visiting.

The plane flagged over Clemson on Wednesday afternoon was monitored by military jets until it landed safely at a nearby airfield, NORAD said, adding that pilots who violate flight restrictions "may also be met by federal authorities upon landing and be subject to enforcement action."

Mr. Trump appeared at Clemson's T. Ed Garrison Arena to address crowds at a campaign rally for Graham, the sister of late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly from a heart condition in July. She took over his role after a special election and is now running for a full term as the Republican nominee in her state's midterm Senate election. Graham is facing Democratic challenger Annie Andrews.

Jets have been scrambled multiple times recently to intercept civilian planes that have violated airspace limitations enacted around Mr. Trump's rallies, which have picked up as the November midterms approach.

Over the weekend, the military command said its F-16s intercepted one aircraft that had entered restricted space over Cincinati, Ohio, on Saturday, while Mr. Trump was speaking at another political rally nearby. Similar incidents were reported by NORAD at the end of September, when Mr. Trump visited Chicago, and in August, when he attended a teen athletic tournament in Geneva, Ohio.

Air Force officials have reminded pilots to be vigilant about checking temporary flight restrictions, which the FAA communicates to them through Notices to Airmen, or NOTAMs, while planning their routes and before taking off.

title: This teacherless school says AI can teach students in 2 hours a day
summary: Alpha Schools says its AI-based instruction and focus on developing "life skills" set students up for success. Some experts say it's too good to be true.
story: Zane Shah arrives at school at 8:45 a.m., greets his friends and stores his backpack in the assigned cubby. It could be any middle school morning. But one thing about Shah's school is different: There are no traditional teachers.

Shah, 13, is an eighth grader at Alpha School, a network of private, for-profit institutions that opened its first Chicago campus this fall for students in pre-K through eighth grade. The adults in the building are called "guides," and artificial intelligence handles all the academic instruction.

When school starts at 9 a.m., students work on math, reading, writing, language and science on laptops, using adaptive software that Alpha says lets them master core subjects in roughly two hours a day.
That mastery doesn't come cheap. Attending Alpha Chicago costs $55,000 a year, or roughly $8,000 more than the average annual cost of a private college, according to U.S. News & World Report.

Alpha was founded in Austin, Texas, in 2014 by MacKenzie Price, who has become an outspoken critic of traditional schooling. Alpha says its students score in the top 1% on national standardized tests. The school also says it does not screen applicants based on previous grades or test scores. Instead, they look for students who are coachable, self-motivated and open to the learning model.
The school says students are only asked to leave for behavioral issues, not failure to meet academic standards.

"They're getting accepted to fantastic schools — Stanford, Northwestern, Rice," said Brian Howell, dean of parents at Alpha Chicago and formerly an anthropology professor at Wheaton College in Illinois.

Shah, who started at Alpha this year, previously attended traditional schools. Two hours of daily academic instruction is enough to accomplish everything he had learned in a typical eight-hour school day, he told CBS News.
"I feel like I can be more focused instead of having 20 to 30 kids in a classroom all talking at once," Shah said.
"Not interacting with chatbots"

Learning at Alpha centers on the school's proprietary educational software, which is used across all of Alpha's campuses and at a handful of affiliated private schools. The system, called TimeBack, was developed by a research team led by cognitive scientist Carl Hendrick of the Netherlands' Academica University of Applied Sciences.

TimeBack is designed to adjust to students' individual skills and capabilities over the course of the school year. For example, if a student repeatedly errs in tackling the same type of problem, the software returns to earlier concepts to fill in any knowledge gaps, according to Alpha.

Alpha also relies on a learning science team comprising subject-matter experts based globally, including licensed teachers, curriculum experts or specialists in early childhood education. They review student data daily, tracking each child's progress and whether they've met their academic goals. The team also builds the curriculum and steps in through remote coaching calls as a last resort if students bog down and need additional help.

Alpha says their approach works more like a private tutor than a chatbot because the software doesn't provide answers; instead, the system is designed to test students' knowledge until it determines they've properly learned a given lesson. The technology is also "closed," meaning it doesn't draw on information from the open internet.
"It's important to understand that they're not interacting with chatbots. They're not getting answers from AI," Howell said.
Replacing teachers with "guides"

Another unusual aspect of Alpha schools is that most guides don't have a background in education. A February analysis from the University of Colorado's National Education Policy Center, a nonpartisan think tank, reported that only about one-third of Alpha guides have education training or degrees.
Carrington Haas, Alpha Chicago's lead guide, told CBS News that staffers at the schools play a different role than traditional teachers.
"We're not teaching academics. The main part of our job is to support the students motivationally and emotionally," she said.
Asked whether guides answer academic questions, Haas added, "No, the academics team has their support so they can jump on a coaching call."
Yet Haas, who has a background in traditional education, including stints at Teach For America and at a Waldorf charter school, rejected the idea that the school is teacherless.
"I think it's the future," she said. "And it's not teacherless because we're still there and we're still very much teaching the life skills that they need to know."

Howell described Alpha's approach as mastery-based, meaning students don't advance until they've demonstrated understanding of a concept. When a student gets stuck, the guide doesn't immediately offer help; instead, it directs the student to reread the problem while drawing on hints from the adaptive software.
"Human beings are looking at those data. They're looking at the dashboards. They're seeing where are students getting stuck, where are they going faster?" Howell said.
Despite Alpha centering its pedagogy on computer-mediated learning, Howell also dismisses any notion that the school's educational approach amounts to parking kids in front of a screen.

"It is not just some mind-numbing, screen-based, zombifying project," he told CBS News. "The AI is not making any decisions about what students learn. The AI's not in control of a student's day — humans are."
So far, Binoy Shah is encouraged by his son's early experience, noting that he quickly noticed a change in Zane's engagement with his education.

"As a 13-year-old kid before you'd get, how was school? Good. How was your lunch? Good. What did you do today? Nothing," Binoy said. "Now we're getting three to five minutes of conversation [about] what he did at school, and he's excited about it."
Experts question Alpha's approach
For all the hype around artificial intelligence, education experts aren't sold on Alpha's unconventional teaching methods and AI-delivered curriculum.

While affirming the value of teaching life skills, such as communication and leadership, Rebecca Winthrop, a senior fellow at the nonpartisan Brookings Institution who has visited Alpha's campuses, questions the school's claims about its educational approach and outcomes. She also urges families who are interested in the school to ensure they know what they're signing up for.
"Parents should know that this is an experimental model. There's no clear externally validated evidence around the results they claim," she said.
"Neuroscience says that deep reflection — meaning-making, which a lot of times schools don't allow enough time for —  is really important for learning and long-term student outcomes," Winthrop added.
Other experts are more bluntly critical of Alpha's approach, accusing the school network of effectively financializing education.

"Alpha School is less an effort to expand educational opportunity than an experiment in extracting maximum profit from schooling," said Carol Corbett Burris, executive director of the Network for Public Education, a nonprofit advocacy group that supports public education.

Burris said Alpha's founders implemented its model at Unbound Academy, a free public charter school in Arizona, built on its TimeBack learning platform. She told CBS News the institution performed "dismally" when compared to Arizona's public schools, "despite the promises submitted in its charter application."

title: John Anderson, country music Hall of Famer, dies at 71
summary: John Anderson, a country music Hall of Famer with a distinctive voice, died on Wednesday, his family said. He was 71 years old.
story: John Anderson, a country music Hall of Famer with a distinctive voice, has died, his family said Wednesday. He was 71 years old.
"It is with the heaviest of hearts that we share the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and best friend," his family said in a statement on Instagram.

"To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives," they said. "To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely, and made every ordinary moment feel special."
"His music will live on, but for us, his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave his family and the memories we will carry with us forever," they said.

Anderson's unmistakable voice helped make him a country music legend. And for some of Nashville's biggest names, he was required listening, with stars like Blake Shelton collaborating with him. Others, including Luke Combs and Ashley McBryde, recorded his songs for his tribute album, "Something Borrowed, Something New."
The Florida native arrived in Nashville as a teenager, playing clubs and working construction — even helping build the roof of the Grand Ole Opry.
But before long, he was the one raising it.
"Swingin'" became a no. 1 hit and the CMA Single of the Year in 1983.
A decade later, "Straight Tequila Night" and "Seminole Wind" brought Anderson's distinctive sound to another generation.
But years later, a mysterious life-threatening illness nearly silenced him, taking away his hearing and leaving him wondering whether he would ever make music again.
Anderson told CBS News in 2022 that the first part of the illness brought severe, terrible headaches, starting in 2016. Then, he said, his hair fell out and he lost his hearing "almost completely."
"They never really figured out just what it was," he said.
His return to music included the 2020 album "Years." Then, in 2024, came country music's highest honor: a place in its Hall of Fame.
"It's a long long road from Apaka, Florida, to standing right here on this stage, but I must say, behind all of that there was a lot of adventure, and I got to choose my own way," he said.
Anderson died just days after attending a Hall of Fame ceremony in Nashville on Sunday.

"I was talking with John Sunday night at the HOF ceremony," country star McGraw wrote on social media. "He was in such good spirits. We talked, we laughed, we sang his songs that I loved so much together, just goofing off. I am completely heartbroken by his passing. There will never be a stylist in music, any music, that was so defining as his."

title: Chemical leak in Toledo forces evacuations, shelter-in-place
summary: A massive chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio, is forcing some people out of their homes while others have been told to shelter in place.
story: A massive chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio, is forcing some people out of their homes while others have been told to shelter in place.
A plume of smoke full of chemicals erupted from the MC Tank terminal.
One injury has been reported so far. According to officials, a Lucas County sheriff's deputy who responded to the scene wasn't feeling well and drove himself to a hospital.
Toledo Fire and Rescue ordered everyone within a 1-mile radius of 1266 Progress Ave. to evacuate, and everyone within a 3-mile radius to shelter in place due to a hazardous materials release.
In an update Wednesday, Toledo officials say the evacuation and shelter-in-place zone has been reduced to half a mile. The orders beyond that zone have been lifted.

"There is still concern that the tank is emitting this chemical, and it has the potential within 12 hours of the incident to be explosive," said Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz. "As a result, our first responders and hazmat teams and safety teams are not approaching the tank."
The evacuation orders were issued at 10:48 p.m. Tuesday, and the shelter-in-place orders were issued at 4:24 a.m. Wednesday.
Those within the shelter-in-place area were asked to stay indoors, close windows and doors and turn off ventilation that draws in outside air. They were also asked to keep pets inside.
MC Tank Transport Inc. said in a statement that equipment associated with its operations is involved in the incident.

According to the statement and as the City of Toledo confirmed, the chemical involved in this incident is glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.
Who is in the evacuation zone?
According to the City of Toledo, the zone is a 1-mile radius around 1266 Progress Ave. Those living or working within 1 mile of that address were asked to evacuate and can go to:
Shoreland Elementary School — temporary shelter.Meijer parking lot (off East Alexis) — Red Cross and TARTA buses are stationed to provide shelter as needed.
Shoreland Elementary School — temporary shelter.

The shelter-in-place zone is a 3-mile radius around 1266 Progress Ave. No injuries have been reported.

title: Candidates clash over Trump policies, Senate control in debate
summary: GOP Sen. Roger Marshall and Pastor Adam Hamilton debated tariffs, war and high fuel prices, and also addressed the most controversial issues in each of their campaigns.
story: The candidates in Kansas' surprisingly competitive Senate race faced off in a debate Wednesday evening, as Republicans fight to head off the possibility of their first loss in a Kansas Senate contest in nearly a century.

Incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall hammered away at what it would mean if he were to lose — that it could help hand control of the Senate to Democrats: "My opponent's going to say anything he can to lie to get into that office and give control to Chuck Schumer."

Marshall's Democratic challenger, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton, tried to convince voters that he's not too progressive for Kansans and went on the offensive against Marshall over the impact of tariffs, the Iran war and other Trump administration policies on the state.
Marshall hewed closely to many of President Trump's views, and like him, blamed rising diesel costs on the war in Ukraine, rather than the Iran war.

"The real problem with the cost of diesel, in particular, is No. 1, is the Ukraine war, and because of that, diesel production has gone down," Marshall said. But at the same time, he said of Mr. Trump's recent announcement that the U.S. would purchase Russian diesel, "it doesn't sound like a great idea to me." He added, "If this brings Russia to the bargaining table and it ends the war, then I'm all for it right now."

While Marshall implored Trump voters to come out and vote for him, he said he does not always align with the president and has "objected" to him multiple times before, specifically citing the ICE raids in Kansas and Mr. Trump's short-term waiver on beef imports, both of which have hurt Kansas farmers.
Hamilton described himself as a "moderate or independent-minded Democrat" and vowed to "work across the aisle to try to bring people together to solve problems."

Hamilton largely sought to distance himself from mainstream Democrats. He promised not to vote for Schumer to be majority leader if Democrats win the Senate, called the Biden administration's border policies a "disaster" and said during a discussion on transgender participation in sports: "I have a 12-year-old granddaughter. I don't want biological men or boys competing against her that could harm her."
Marshall argued Hamilton leans further to the left than he has let on. The Republican senator also questioned how independent Hamilton would be.

"He's going to say he's going to vote against these things, but every Democrat stands up, and when Schumer tells them to jump, they say, 'how high?'" Marshall said during the sports discussion. "So why is he going to be any different once he gets to Washington? He can tell us one thing, but let's see what his actions would be like."

Hamilton said he would try to "force" Mr. Trump to end the Iran war. High gas prices and tariffs are putting many farms in the state in dire economic straits, with many voters telling CBS News that they aren't sure if they will survive past next year if conditions continue.
"It was not a good decision to go to war in Iran, and we need to get out," said Hamilton.

Marshall said he "want[s] this war to be over … as soon as possible, but we cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon." He described Hamilton's views as "war through weakness, as opposed to peace through strength."
Hamilton slammed Mr. Trump's tariffs, arguing they have led to chaos and uncertainty. Marshall said the president's tariffs have led to a "manufacturing renaissance."

Mr. Trump's immigration policies have also drawn scrutiny in Kansas, including a string of Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids that agricultural leaders warned could cause workforce disruptions. Marshall pushed back last month, saying in a post on social media that ICE "needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement."

During Wednesday's debate, Hamilton called ICE's practices "militarized" and "politicized." Marshall said "all this discussion starts with a secure border," arguing Democrats could loosen border enforcement.
Polling suggests a tight race, and millions of dollars have gushed into Kansas, flooding the state's airwaves with anti-Marshall and anti-Hamilton ads.

The debate's moderator wasted no time in asking both candidates about their biggest controversies. For Marshall, that's the New York Times report about how the OB/GYN aggressively pursued his former patients — many of whom struggled economically — for medical debts and in some cases had them arrested.
Hamilton faced questions regarding his church's response to an incident of child sex abuse at a youth summer camp in 2005.

Marshall said "we did everything possible to take good care of people" and that many of his patients got free care. He conceded that some patients were turned over to collections agencies, which he called a fairly rare occurrence that is standard in the medical industry.

At his rally in Wichita on Monday, Mr. Trump defended Marshall against these allegations, saying he was required by law to report the debt, and that he's been unfairly "made out to be some kind of Shylock character." (The Anti-Defamation League later said the term "Shylock," a reference to a Jewish moneylender in William Shakespeare's "The Merchant of Venice," is "rooted in a longstanding antisemitic stereotype.")

On the abuse scandal, Hamilton said his church subsequently changed its policy on handling allegations of abuse, and "ultimately, we helped get this man put behind bars." Still, Hamilton admitted, "I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back (to the youth camp). That was a mistake on my part."
Cathy Bien, a spokesperson for Hamilton's United Methodist Church, told CBS News on Wednesday that the incident was "handled the best way [they] knew how 20 years ago."

Kansas could decide which party controls the Senate, and even before the debate, early voting numbers were skyrocketing in the state. Election officials say that they are fielding numbers that rival the 2024 presidential election.

The race could hinge on how many Republicans cross party lines to vote for Hamilton. At least 100 Kansas Republican leaders have endorsed Hamilton, including former governors, state officials and Mr. Trump's own former White House press secretary, Stephanie Grisham.

But many are voting early to ensure Republicans maintain control of the Senate. One early voter in Wichita, Tim Higgins, told CBS News that he's backing Marshall because "it's important to keep the progress that the nation is currently on since the presidential election."
However, for many, the race is about state issues.
"Rural Kansas is struggling, urban Kansas is struggling," said former Republican state Rep. Terrie Huntington, who is voting for Hamilton. "I think people are looking for change."

title: Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers clash in final Michigan Senate debate
summary: Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed clashed onstage Wednesday during the second debate in the increasingly bitter Michigan Senate race.
story: Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed clashed onstage Wednesday during the second, and final, debate in the increasingly bitter Michigan Senate race. El-Sayed repeatedly argued his opponent is and would be a "sock puppet" for President Trump in the Senate, while Rogers cast his opponent as untrustworthy and trying to run from past, further-left positions.

The neck-and-neck race is one of the nation's most closely watched contests in the November midterms and could help determine which party wins control of the Senate. Democrats hope to take advantage of Mr. Trump's unpopularity and voters' frustration with inflation and the Iran War. Republicans have sought to capitalize on divisions between progressives like El-Sayed and more moderate Democrats on Middle East policy and Medicare for All.

El-Sayed called Rogers' platform a "MAGA vision" and argued the former congressman "stand[s] hip-to-hip with Donald Trump on all of his worst policies, the policies that are raising the price of your gas, making it impossible to afford your groceries." The Democratic former health official responded to attack lines by inviting the audience to play "MAGA bingo."
"He's going to bend to Donald Trump because he is a sock puppet for the man," said El-Sayed.
Rogers pushed back at one point, saying: "He wants to make this about Donald Trump. The bingo game ought to be: 'How many times can he put Trump in any answer?'"
Asked by reporters after the debate if he's planning to attend Mr. Trump's Michigan rally on Sunday, which El-Sayed brought up, Rogers said he'd go but didn't know all the final details yet.
During the debate, Rogers argued El-Sayed has not been honest about his platform, accusing him of engaging in a "pattern of deception."

"Think about this: there are so many Democrats who are coming out today and saying they can't vote for Abdul El-Sayed because he's too extreme," Rogers said. He also claimed he's "doing exceptionally well with Jewish Democrats who are literally afraid," alluding to some community members' reluctance to support El-Sayed, a frequent critic of the Israeli government.
The debate was somewhat tamer than the two candidates' first faceoff earlier this month, which featured insults and interruptions in virtually every answer. But it was still testy.

One of the more contentious moments came after Rogers tried to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood and suggested he had the same supporters as terror groups like Hamas — allegations El-Sayed has vehemently pushed back against.

Earlier this month, several news outlets reported on social media posts by El-Sayed's half sister suggesting the Democratic candidate's mother had supported the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group and political movement founded in her home country of Egypt.

El-Sayed has disavowed any connection to the organization, and has noted that he wasn't raised by his birthmother since his parents divorced when he was young. Rogers said El-Sayed was trying to make himself look like "a victim."

"You can grin and you can smile and you can talk real pretty, but I'm going to tell you what, that is a risk to our national security," Rogers said. He told reporters after the debate that he questions whether El-Sayed can get a security clearance if elected.
El-Sayed called the allegations "shameful."

"He keeps raising this question about this association with an organization I've never been a part of, because [of] my mom, who's a nurse in Missouri?" the Democrat said. "It doesn't make any sense, and it's actually really quite beneath you, Mike."
El-Sayed pressed Rogers on the Iran war, pointing to the conflict as the cause of high consumer prices and casting the Republican as a hawk who has "a war for everything."

"We need a War Powers Resolution, rather than a senator who is going to stand hip-to-hip with Donald Trump on this war that made no sense when it started and certainly makes no sense now," El-Sayed said when asked how he would bring costs down.
Rogers has called on the war to end, but also said on the debate stage that if Iran is allowed to control the Strait of Hormuz or build a nuclear weapon that gas could rise even higher.

The moderators asked El-Sayed whether he views Iran as a significant threat to U.S. national security. It was a variation on a question during the first debate, when El-Sayed was asked whether Iran or Israel is a bigger threat, which he called a "ridiculous hypothetical."

El-Sayed said Wednesday that "there's no doubt that Iran has posed a threat," but he argued "that threat had been contained" by the Obama-era deal that limited Iran's nuclear program. Mr. Trump ended that deal during his first term in office.
Rogers said Iran is "absolutely" a threat and argued El-Sayed's previous answers on Iran were "an absolute nonstarter if you're going to send somebody … to the United States Senate."
Meanwhile, Rogers pushed El-Sayed on some of his progressive policy views, including his support for Medicare for All, a single-payer healthcare plan.
"Money in your pocket? You'll be lucky to have a damn pair of pants when you're done," said Rogers, arguing El-Sayed's policies would require significant tax hikes.

El-Sayed responded by saying: "Right now, the folks pulling the money out of your pocket are the big corporations who are buying his campaign." Asked by CBS News after the debate about how much the plan would cost, El-Sayed argued if implemented it'd be less expensive than the costs of healthcare currently, and said the platform has bipartisan support.
On tariffs, El-Sayed criticized Mr. Trump's tariffs but said he is open to some import duties. He said, "You don't give all the chemo all at once, all at the same time."
Rogers called the president's tariffs a "mixed bag," questioning the trade war with Canada but saying the "reshoring of manufacturing is underway."

title: Judge curbs DHS efforts to conduct sweeps for possible noncitizen voters
summary: A federal judge ruled DHS's practice of knocking on doors and asking people about their immigration status — and whether they have voted in recent elections — likely violates the Voting Rights Act.
story: A federal judge ruled late Wednesday that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's practice of knocking on doors and asking people about their immigration status — and whether they have voted in recent elections — likely violates the Voting Rights Act.

The ruling took aim at an operation that was documented by a CBS News investigation earlier Wednesday. Homeland Security Investigations has posted photos and videos of agents approaching homes in multiple states. The Trump administration says the practice is part of an effort to crack down on voting by noncitizens, but critics say it could intimidate legal voters.

In her ruling, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin ordered federal immigration authorities to stop carrying out "elections-related field operations and field interviews" in nine states, including California and New York, if the operations are likely to involve people who government officials "know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens."
Her order will remain in effect until polls close on Election Day. She stayed the ruling until 5 p.m. on Friday, which will give the government a chance to seek appeal.

Martinez-Olguin sided with groups that sued over the noncitizen voting investigation surge, including the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United. She found the policy likely ran afoul of a section of the Voting Rights Act that makes it illegal to "intimidate, threaten, or coerce" those who assist people with voting or engage in voter mobilization efforts.

"Plaintiffs do not claim, nor does the Court find, that it is unlawful for federal officials to undertake investigations into unlawful voting in federal elections," the judge wrote. "Rather, Plaintiffs seek to stop DHS from continuing to investigate U.S. citizens, who have a legal right to vote, in a way that intimidates and threatens the participation of CNA/NNU members from urging or aiding others to vote."

Martinez-Olguin also pointed to the "high likelihood of error" in the government's process for assembling a list of potential targets, which includes data from government agencies and commercially available data.
Protect Democracy, one of the groups that sued over the policy, celebrated the ruling.

"It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people's homes weeks before an election," Beau Tremitiere, counsel at Protect Democracy, said in a statement to CBS News. "Today's ruling should remind us that American citizens hold the ultimate power in our democracy, not the government–no matter what the administration says otherwise."
CBS News has reached out to DHS for comment.

President Trump has prioritized cracking down on voter fraud during his second term, although there has been little evidence to back up his claims of widespread voting by noncitizens. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Justice Department.
The Justice Department reported earlier this week that it arrested several dozen green card holders in California on allegations they illegally registered to vote in U.S. federal elections.

title: On dating apps, men use AI to put their best face forward
summary: How much AI is too much when it comes to finding love on the apps? "It's very subtle," one dating app user said of his AI-enhanced photos.
story: Marissa, a 31-year-old Boston resident, downloaded dating apps because she is looking for love. But more and more, she finds herself looking for something else: AI-free photos.

The marketing professional said she routinely comes across dating app profiles that appear to be digitally altered. Usually, the changes are minor and can be easily made using tools like Photoshop, such as editing someone out of a photo. Sometimes, however, the photo appears to be completely AI-generated, she told CBS News, citing a photo she came across on Bumble of a man dressed in a suit tiling a bathroom wall.
"AI aside, I'm not sure what the appeal is there," she said (Marissa asked to withhold her surname for privacy reasons).

Numerous women on TikTok also report spotting photos of men on dating apps that appear to be AI-generated. Their accounts demonstrate how AI is blurring the line between what's real and what's fake in the already fraught arena of online dating. They also raise ethical questions about how far is too far when it comes to manipulating your online persona.

"People want authentic connections and conversations," Kathryn Coduto, an assistant professor at Boston University who studies dating apps, told CBS News in an email. "I think AI has made people more wary and skeptical of others, especially people they don't know."

Of course, dating app users have long relied on filters and other editing tools to polish their photos. But AI tools are upping the ante, allowing people to create high-quality images within seconds, and in some cases, fabricate fake scenes.

"A dater has to think about how they're going to capture someone's attention in a few seconds or less," Coduto told CBS News. "This might mean making your photo look a little better than it might have before."
To be sure, this practice isn't exclusive to men. However, they appear more likely to use AI to spruce up their dating profiles than women, Coduto added.
"So far, men are more interested in AI in the dating space, which isn't surprising," Coduto said. "Women tend to receive more matches and messages, so men have a harder time standing out."
The "digital stylist" who helps men AI their photos

AI can create obvious distortions when it generates photos, such as omitting a finger from someone's hand. For Marissa, a telltale sign is the person's face, which sometimes looks "waxy" in AI-generated photos, she said.
Still, as technology improves, it's becoming harder to distinguish a real photo from one created by AI models.

Lana Li, a Brooklyn, New York, dating consultant who runs the Substack "Love Me Like a Robot," calls herself a "digital stylist." She uses AI to help men level up their dating app photos, and defends using the technology as long as the photos still genuinely represent who they are.

"I can take a picture of somebody and then put them in a different outfit or change their hairstyle a little bit, or put different shoes on them," she told CBS News. "Or if I think their body language doesn't look confident in the picture, I will have [ChatGPT] change that."
The 37-year-old also uses FaceApp to change men's facial expressions. She said the edits are subtle, such as slightly lifting the corner of someone's mouth to make them look "friendlier."

Despite her liberal approach to using AI, there are lines Li is unwilling to cross. For example, one client asked her to digitally alter a photo so that his head was on a marathon runner's body — a request she declined.
"I told him, 'I can't work with you if you want to not represent yourself accurately,'" she said.

Two men who spoke to CBS News on the condition of anonymity to maintain their privacy told CBS News they've used AI in their online dating photos, but in ways they feel stop short of being misleading and remain true to who they are.
A ban on Hinge
One man, a 30-year-old tech employee and client of Li's, said she used ChatGPT to digitally clothe him in more professional garb and to tame his frizzy hair.

"It's very subtle," the New York City resident said, saying he still looked like himself, even with the edits. He emphasized that he doesn't want to "catfish" anyone — a concern for singles even in the absence of AI.

Another man is pulling back after one of his AI photos backfired. The 50-something-year-old New York City resident said he fed photos of himself into Aragon.ai, an AI headshot generator, which produced a picture of him standing on a Manhattan roof with a sunset in the background. It immediately drew hits on his Hinge profile.

"This picture generally got the most likes," he told CBS News. "Now that could just be because it was the first thing they saw. But regardless, it was proving to be effective, and women seemed to like it."
That was, until Hinge banned him. He managed to get his account back but ultimately decided to delete the sunset photo, suspecting it was the reason for his removal from the app.
"How much AI am I OK with?"

Most popular dating apps have policies that limit the use of AI-generated images in people's profiles. Hinge emphasizes the importance of authenticity on its website, noting that people should be able to discern "fact from fiction."
"If you decide to include generative AI images, audio, or video in your profile, it should not be used to misrepresent yourself or your intentions," the company says on its AI policy page.

Hinge also uses automated tools and human reviewers to detect and remove "prohibited material," according to the company's terms of service. If users see suspicious AI material, they can confidentially report it through the app or online.

A spokesperson for Match Group, which owns Hinge, Tinder and a handful of other dating apps, told CBS that as generative AI evolves, the company is "watching closely and listening to daters, who tell us they want more transparency, more authenticity, and more confidence that a real person is on the other end."

Bumble also uses tools to detect and weed out AI-generated content, and lets users report profiles that feature such images. A spokesperson said the company prohibits inauthentic profiles, and Bumble's community guidelines bar the use of "artificially generated photos or enhanced photos to deceive others."

"We enforce this through a combination of AI-powered tools, human moderation, verification features and member reporting, and we take action based on the severity of a violation, up to and including permanently banning accounts," the spokesperson said.
Marissa, the 31-year-old who lives in Boston, said that when she sees a person's profile whose photos bear the hallmarks of AI, she chooses to move along.
"The dating pool is already challenging, and this is just another thing we have to grapple with," she said. "How much AI am I OK with?"

title: Man who halted runaway school bus credits "Grey's Anatomy" inspiration
summary: A quick-thinking bystander came to the rescue of the students and driver aboard a runaway school bus in Saint Paul, Minnesota.
story: A quick-thinking man who came to the rescue of the students and driver aboard a runaway school bus in Saint Paul, Minnesota, on Monday afternoon credited the television series "Grey's Anatomy" for inspiring his actions.
Ebro Ahmed, 27, told CBS News that he leaped into action after noticing the Battle Creek Middle School bus rolling down the street at about 10 mph with its doors wide open and its lights flashing.
Ahmed said it caught his attention because the lights of a school bus normally don't flash unless it is at a complete stop.
"When he drove past me, it really shook me," Ahmed told CBS News Wednesday. "I was like, 'What is going on?'"
As captured on nearby security cameras, Ahmed, who works at a nearby store, sprinted from the sidewalk and jumped onto the moving bus.
"I saw the bus driver obviously having a medical emergency," Ahmed said. "All I looked at was the gear control and I was trying to put it into park."

Ahmed, who told CBS News he had never been behind the wheel of a bus before, said he briefly got confused between the reverse and park selections on the gear shift and accidentally put the bus into reverse.
"I started hearing beeps and we were going backwards," Ahmed explained. "And then I said, 'That is not right,' and I threw it into neutral and pulled the [parking] brake."
He went on: "When I looked behind me, I saw all of the kids kind of a little scared, crying with their phones out getting ready to call the police."
Saint Paul Public Schools said there were 19 students aboard the bus at the time. None of them were hurt in the incident. The district did not provide information on the condition of the driver.

"After everything, he was coming to, but he's still kind of out of it," Ahmed said of the driver. "And so I just let him be. Even when the police came, he was already done having his medical emergency. He was getting a little bit better, but I just didn't want to rush and start asking him questions."
Ahmed doesn't have any medical experience, but he does credit his favorite TV show, "Grey's Anatomy," for inspiring him.
"In 'Grey's Anatomy,' you never see doctors panic. I know it is all acting and stuff, so I just knew to be calm and just think everything through," Ahmed said.
The district said a second bus eventually came to pick up the students and continue the route.
Asked if he feels like a hero, Ahmed responded, "I feel like any person in my situation would have done the same thing."

title: First case of New World screwworm found in U.S. wildlife, USDA says
summary: The New World screwworm was detected in an elk that was discovered on a game ranch in Pecos County, Texas.
story: The first case of New World screwworm in wildlife in the United States has been found in an elk in Texas, the U.S. Department of Agriculture announced Wednesday.
The elk was discovered on a game ranch in Pecos County and was reported after being harvested by a hunter, the USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service said.

The detection prompted additional wildlife surveillance in the area by the USDA and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department. The Texas Animal Health Commission will also modify a previously established infested zone.
Officials said hunters should watch for signs of infection, including visible maggots in wounds, foul-smelling injuries and animals that appear weak or distressed.
Other warning signs include open or enlarging wounds and infestations around an animal's nose, mouth, ears, eyes or genital areas.
Officials urged anyone who notices suspicious signs of infestation to report them immediately.
The USDA in June confirmed the presence of a flesh-eating New World screwworm in a 3-week-old Texas calf.

New World screwworm is a parasitic fly that lays eggs in open wounds or body openings of warm-blooded animals, including livestock and, in rare cases, humans. Once hatched, the larvae feed on living tissue, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
While the USDA says New World screwworm doesn't affect food safety, it can impact meat production.

Typically found in South America and parts of the Caribbean, the parasite has spread north into Central America and Mexico in recent years. The first human case in the U.S. was confirmed last year, though the patient recovered and officials found no evidence of further transmission.

title: Teacher who survived Oregon school shooting recounts playing dead
summary: Becky Drury, the 54-year-old teacher wounded in the shooting at an Oregon elementary school last week, says she was shot before she had "any chance to act."
story: Becky Drury, the 54-year-old teacher wounded in the shooting at an Oregon elementary school last week, is sharing a statement about her experience, saying the gunman shot her before she had "any chance to act."
In the statement Wednesday, Drury recalled running to see what was happening outside her classroom at Silver Rail Elementary School before spotting the shooter.
"I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there," Drury wrote. "Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground."

"Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured," she continued. "I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else. So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again."

Drury suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries from the Oct. 15 shooting that killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher. Another student, a 7-year-old, was also seriously wounded.

The suspect was identified as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a former student at the school. Police said he shot through the school's locked doors before entering a special needs classroom and opening fire.
The gunman was tackled by another teacher and fatally shot by an armed bystander, 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco, who followed him into the school, according to police.
Drury said Wednesday she was sharing what happened to her because "I want to make sure the events of that day and my actions in particular are reported accurately."
"I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act," she wrote.

She thanked those who have supported her since the shooting, and said, "What happened in that classroom was unimaginable, and like so many in this community, my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy."

title: Witkoff blasted for calling Putin a "humanitarian"
summary: After special envoy Steve Witkoff told Putin he was a "humanitarian" for releasing a U.S. citizen deemed to have been wrongfully detained, GOP Sen. John Cornyn responded, "No. Putin is a stone cold killer."
story: Washington — U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff faced immediate backlash Wednesday for praising Russian President Vladimir Putin as a "humanitarian" after he released 74-year-old Stephen Hubbard, an American who had been imprisoned in Russia for four years and who had been determined to be wrongfully detained.

"You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian," Witkoff told Putin Wednesday in response to Hubbard's release. "You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again."

Witkoff made the comment in St. Petersburg during a visit with the Russian president that was aimed at moving toward a resolution of the Ukraine war that Putin started four and a half years ago. Over the past month, Russia has been intensifying its strikes against civilian and energy infrastructure to try to cripple the power grid before the brutal Ukrainian winter.

Mr. Trump was asked later in the day if he would describe Putin the same way Witkoff did. "Well, I guess you have to say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out," Mr. Trump said during a White House roundtable on cyber crime. "But I wouldn't say anything one way or the other."
Witkoff's "humanitarian" comment sparked pushback from Republicans, some of whom have openly criticized the president and his administration in recent months.

"WTF, Steve?" wrote North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. "Look up the definition of 'humanitarian.' What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say. You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a 'humanitarian.'"
Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas responded to a video of Witkoff's comments: "No. Putin is a stone cold killer," he wrote on X.
"Another embarrassment," said Republican Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who has been critical of the Trump administration's handling of Russia and Ukraine.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, who has also been critical of the administration, was asked about the comment on the campaign trail and replied, "I would describe Putin as a warmonger, a thug. He's certainly not a humanitarian. He is the aggressor in the war against Ukraine."

Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine William Taylor, who served during the Bush and Obama administrations, said in an interview with CBS News that it's "absolutely a good thing" Hubbard is coming home, "but he should never have been there in the first place."
"We should not give the Russians any credit for releasing someone who should not have been in jail," Taylor said. "And to call Putin a humanitarian, that's cringeworthy."
Republican Sen. Joni Ernst of Iowa said Putin is "not our friend."

"Vladimir Putin is not our friend, and he is certainly no humanitarian," she posted on X. "His relentless attacks on innocent civilians in Ukraine show his total disregard for human life.   Appeasement won't end this war. Pressure will."

Witkoff's praise of Putin also comes as Mr. Trump made the surprise move last week to waive new U.S. sanctions on Russia two days before they were supposed to go into effect, defying Congress and his late friend, Sen. Lindsey Graham. The waivers came one week after Mr. Trump had eased sanctions on Russian diesel and announced a deal with Putin to import diesel to the U.S. market.
Mr. Trump has expressed increasing frustration with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and on Tuesday, said "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much."
Before heading to Russia, Witkoff was in Oslo, Norway, where he met with and embraced Zelenskyy. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described that meeting as "positive."

title: New Mexico AG accuses Epstein's lawyer, accountant of concealing crimes
summary: New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez filed a lawsuit Wednesday against two of Jeffrey Epstein's closest confidants, attorney Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn.
story: The New Mexico attorney general filed a lawsuit Wednesday against two of Jeffrey Epstein's closest confidants, seeking to stop them from receiving payments for serving as executors of his estate.
The lawsuit claims attorney Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn "facilitated and concealed" sex trafficking by Epstein at his Zorro Ranch, outside Santa Fe.

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement announcing the suit that "Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible."

"The allegations in this lawsuit describe a network of people and financial arrangements that helped sustain and conceal the abuse of vulnerable girls and young women, including here in New Mexico," Torrez said. "Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences."

Indyke and Kahn said in March testimonies before Congress that they were unaware of Epstein's crimes, beyond a 2008 guilty plea on prostitution charges. Lawyers for the men said Wednesday that they "emphatically reject the New Mexico Attorney General's allegations that they were complicit in or in any way knowingly facilitated Mr. Epstein's sexual abuse or trafficking – conduct that by all accounts occurred behind closed doors, in secluded locations, and at times when neither Mr. Indyke nor Mr. Kahn was present."

"Neither the New Mexico Attorney General nor anyone from his office asked to speak with Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn to seek relevant information from them before filing this baseless lawsuit, raising serious questions about the thoroughness of the Attorney General's investigation and the motivations for his lawsuit," they said.

Indyke worked closely with Epstein for decades, and Kahn for more than 10 years, before Epstein's 2019 death in a federal jail, where he was being held on charges of sex trafficking minors. The medical examiner determined his death was suicide.

The lawsuit claims Indyke and Kahn were central to "an informal network of associates bound together by a single purpose: knowingly facilitating and concealing his decades-long criminal conduct to preserve and grow Epstein's fortunes and influence."

Survivors of Epstein's abuse have claimed Indyke and Kahn were key figures in the management of dozens of interconnected companies used to make payments on Epstein's behalf. The men recently settled a lawsuit in which they were accused of facilitating sham marriages in which foreign-born victims married Americans whom Epstein abused, for immigration purposes.
Six survivors lauded the New Mexico lawsuit in a statement Wednesday.

"Those who argue that [Epstein] could not have acted alone are right. His operation depended on the appearance of legitimacy and access to money carefully structured to avoid exposing his crimes," said Marina Lacerda, Anouska De Georgiou, Julia Molchanova, Courtney Wild, Jena Lisa Jones and Chauntae Davies. "This lawsuit is aimed at the two men most responsible for that appearance and structure."

Epstein purchased Zorro Ranch in 1993, building a mansion, airstrip and helipad on the property. He was under investigation in the state at the time of his death and Torrez reopened the investigation this year.

title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion to New Mexico in data privacy ruling
summary: A jury found that the social media company had deceived consumers for years about its data privacy policies.
story: Meta has been ordered by a judge in New Mexico to pay $25 billion to the state after a jury found that the social media company deceived consumers for years about its data privacy policies.

Judge Francis Mathew handed down the amount, which New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez described as "one of the largest, if not the single largest state verdict against a company in American history."
"This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley," Torrez said in a news conference.

In September, jury members found that Facebook had made false or misleading statements by telling consumers that they controlled how their information was shared. The social media giant also misled consumers by claiming it didn't sell or share personal information with advertisers, the jury concluded.

The jury found that the company's "most senior leadership," including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and former chief operating officer Sheryl Sandberg, made misrepresentations about the service's data privacy policies, the judge ruled.
"These communications were part of a coherent strategy designed to mislead the public," Mathew wrote.

The case stemmed from allegations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads.
In a statement on Wednesday, Torrez said that the case "has always been about more than one company or one scandal."
He added, "It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences."
C.J. Mahoney, Meta's Chief Legal Officer, said in a statement that the company is confident it will "prevail on appeal."

"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."
Where the $25 billion could go
Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws are funneled toward state education spending.
"We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," Torrez said, while noting that the money would be tied up if Meta appeals the decision, as expected.
Forty-eight other states settled with Facebook in a nationwide case, but New Mexico chose to take the social media company to court on its own.
Attorneys for New Mexico had sought $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing that the company would only change its ways with a sum large enough to affect its stock price.
Lawyers for Meta said the company should pay no more than $3.4 billion, arguing that a much larger award would violate due process, be unconstitutional and not hold up on appeal.
In 2019, the Federal Trade Commission hit Facebook, then called Meta, with a $5 billion fine over its role in allowing Cambridge Analytica to collect users' data without their consent.
Meta argued that New Mexico failed to prove that the tech giant's executives made misleading statements about privacy and that its content moderation practices harmed state residents.
Shares of Meta rose $13.56, or 2%, to $707.81 in Wednesday afternoon trading.

title: Childcare costs are growing faster than rent in the U.S.
summary: A growing share of American families are having to shell out more than $2,000 a month for childcare services, new data shows.
story: The rising cost of childcare in the U.S. is vying with food prices and healthcare expenses in straining household budgets.

Nearly 8% of families are spending more than $2,000 per month on childcare services, including daycare, nanny services and other programs. That's more than double the share of households that spent that much just three years ago, according to new research from the Bank of America Institute.

In September, the cost of daycare and school-related fees rose faster than other essential expenses, such as rent and medical care, compared to the same period a year ago, according to federal labor data.

Families nationwide spent an average of 8% of their monthly incomes on childcare services in September, BofA found. Under federal guidelines, childcare is considered affordable when it consumes no more than 7% of household income.

Assuming a family spends $24,000 annually on childcare, it would need to earn roughly $343,000 to remain below the 7% threshold. In 2025, median household income was $87,460, according to Census Bureau data.
Lower- and middle-income families spend nearly 9% of their annual incomes on childcare payments, while higher-income households spend 7.3%, according to BofA.

Along with facing rising childcare costs, workers have also seen slowing wage growth, heightening the financial pressure on many families, Economic Policy Institute economist Elise Gould told CBS News.
Separate research from AARP shows that families are turning to grandparents, who provide $172 billion per year in direct financial assistance.
Where are childcare costs growing fastest?

In some parts of the U.S., childcare fees are rising even faster, according to BofA. In September, median childcare costs rose fastest in Nashville, Tennessee, followed by Jacksonville, Florida, and Phoenix, Arizona, compared to the same period a year ago, according to BofA's analysis.

"There's been an increase in domestic migration to these areas," BofA Institute economist Taylor Bowley told CBS News, noting that an increase in demand for childcare services is putting pressure on prices.

A shortage of childcare workers also appears to be driving up childcare expenses. Employment in the sector fell 0.7% in September compared to one year earlier, making it harder for providers to deliver such services.
"You see job growth falling and price pressures creeping in, leading to a bit of an availability problem," BofA Institute senior economist David Tinsley told CBS News.

A lack of affordable childcare disproportionately affects women's employment opportunities, according to the researchers. Women are more likely than men to take on childcare responsibilities, according to data from the American Time Use Survey.
"Beyond childcare being a household expense, it's a form of economic enablement," Bowley said.

title: Armed federal agents knock on doors looking for noncitizen voters
summary: Armed and in uniform, agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors to ask residents about their immigration status whether they're registered to vote.
story: Armed and in uniform, federal agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors in several states to ask residents about their immigration status — and to inquire if they have registered to vote or cast votes in past elections, a CBS News Investigation has found.

The operation is part of an effort to root out potential noncitizen voters ahead of the midterms. DHS has alleged that there could be as many as 250,000 citizens illegally registered to vote, although election experts have disputed the accuracy of this figure. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Department of Justice. There are 227 million registered voters in the U.S.
Critics say that sending armed federal agents to the doors of U.S. residents could be intimidating for legal voters.

"What we're seeing now is the federal government is inserting itself into the state process for verifying their voter roles in an unprecedented way," said Jessica Marsden, a lawyer for Protect Democracy, a left-leaning advocacy group that is suing the federal agency over the door-knocking campaign. "And they are doing it in a way that seems maximally designed to scare lawful voters from participating."

The home visits ramped up in September, in the thick of the midterm campaign season, and continued over the past weekend. The Justice Department announced Monday that Homeland Security agents in California arrested more than 20 people, all of them green card holders, on allegations they had illegally registered or cast a vote.

As part of that roundup, dozens of federal agents descended on the residence of a 72-year-old man from Belize, who was taken from his home in his pajamas and arrested on charges he allegedly voted illegally in the past four elections.

"HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found," said a DHS spokesperson. "Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders."
Eric Balliet, a former Homeland Security Investigations agent, said the door-knocking operation is a significant departure from traditional law enforcement activities.

"In my 23 years with HSI, I never engaged in or was aware of any incident or initiative that sent Special Agents to private residences to verify the eligibility of voters," Balliet said, who served in the federal government under multiple administrations.

In June, the DHS directed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, to assist in deportations of alleged noncitizen voters. Homeland Security Investigations, the agency conducting the at-home visits, is one of the enforcement arms of ICE and typically focuses on criminal cross border investigations like child exploitation, drug smuggling and money laundering.

Months later after the announcement, hundreds of agents were pulled off their cases and assigned to track down alleged noncitizen voters as part of a "surge" initiative, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. The directive, first reported by CNN, describes a "Criminal Voter Fraud " initiative that includes "field reviews" in at least six states including California, Georgia, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

Photos and videos posted on X show agents from Homeland Security Investigations, some of whom are carrying firearms, approaching houses and knocking on doors, under captions like, "AMERICAN ELECTIONS ARE FOR AMERICANS."
One photo from Kansas City HSI's account shows four agents at the door of a woman standing on her porch holding a child's hand.

The woman is identified in a Department of Justice press release as Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a Peruvian national who was charged with four counts of voter-fraud related crimes including illegally casting a ballot in the 2024 election. Her case has not yet been heard. Her lawyer declined to respond to CBS News' request for comment.

Hours after this article was published, Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson, the ranking member of the Homeland Security Committee, wrote to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to demand the that DHS immediately cease "law enforcement activity aimed at intimidating the public as the 2026 midterm elections are underway." He said the DHS operations "reflect an anti-democratic departure from the mission Congress set for the Department, and serve only President Trump's voter suppression agenda, not a legitimate enforcement objective."
For civil rights advocates, the show of force has sparked concerns about the chilling effect it could have on legal voters.
"It is sending the signal to a much broader community, do not show up at the polls. Do not vote," said Dr. Carol Anderson, a professor of African American Studies at Emory University.

"And so if you are somebody who has registered to vote and you're a naturalized citizen, what you see in that community is that —  because this is not a regime that makes those discernments — that you're gonna stay away from the voting booth."

A DHS spokesperson said, "DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens. … Those who are here legally and are not breaking other laws have nothing to fear."
"Target List"
In one video, agents are filmed holding a document that says, "Target List."

That list can be far reaching, said a HSI agent familiar with the initiative who asked to speak anonymously. DHS pulls from internal databases, voter rolls, and other datasets. Then employees attempt to match names against citizenship data provided by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, or USCIS.

In September, a USCIS whistleblower said that employees were asked to review the voter information of tens of thousands of individuals across the country, including citizens. Employees were given quotas to investigate 40 subjects a day, which is a rate of roughly 12 minutes per subject.
DHS has defended the data matching program and the work USCIS has done to identify potential noncitizen voters.

"Far from being rushed or untrained, these investigative efforts are conducted diligently and professionally,"  said a DHS spokesperson. "There is no quota on criminality. DHS will pursue each and every illegal voter to the fullest extent of the law ."
"There's every reason to expect that there are many, many more false positives in these lists," said Marsden.

She noted that Homeland Security officials initially said they had identified nearly 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada's voter rolls, but ultimately they were unable to provide evidence of a single illegally registered voter.

title: Electricity bills force 1 in 5 to cut back on food, survey finds
summary: Americans living on a fixed income are particularly vulnerable when electricity costs surge, a Consumer Reports expert says.
story: About one in five Americans say they have had to cut back on groceries to afford their electricity bills, while roughly a quarter of consumers are turning down their heating or air conditioning to uncomfortable levels to lower their energy costs, according to a new survey from Consumer Reports.

About 80% of people who have lived in the same home for at least three years say their electricity bills have increased over that time, according to a national survey of more than 2,000 adults by the nonprofit advocacy group. The largest share, 28%, said their bills had surged between 20% and 49% over that period.
Electricity prices across major U.S. cities have jumped 14% over the last three years, according to federal data.

Rising utility costs are worsening the affordability crunch facing millions of American families, who are facing sharply higher gasoline and diesel prices amid higher oil costs due to the war in Iran. The survey found that consumers are cutting back where they can, such as switching to less expensive foods or spending less on discretionary items, to cope with rising electricity bills.

"We're hearing a lot of folks who don't know what they can possibly do to afford rising [electricity] rates," Sara Enright, senior director of safety and energy at Consumer Reports, told CBS News. "Vulnerable populations like students and retirees who live on a fixed income don't have a lot of flex in their budgets, and so when they get a surprise bill in the heat of the summer, it can be frightening."
Consumers often prioritize paying their utility bills because they need to keep their lights on and their refrigerators running, she added.
"People are cutting back on food" to pay their utility bills, Enright said. "They're definitely cutting back on non-essentials like vacations and eating out."

Other polls show that energy costs are weighing on voters ahead of next month's midterm elections, along with other cost-of-living issues. The cost of food is the top concern for voters in battleground states, followed by gas prices and utility bills, according to an October survey from Climate Power, a clean energy advocacy group.
"Increasingly distrustful"

Consumer Reports found that Americans blame their higher electric bills on utility companies seeking to maximize profits and on the rapid buildout of data centers. Electricity demand is forecast to increase 16% by 2029, mainly due to the proliferation of data centers across the U.S., according to energy management company Schneider Electric.

The price of natural gas, ongoing electrification of buildings and vehicles, and other factors are also contributing to rising power costs. Meanwhile, a majority of respondents said they don't believe state utility regulators are protecting their interests, Consumer Reports found.

"The public is becoming increasingly distrustful that government is looking out for them, and this is true across party lines," Enright told CBS News. "Everyday people, as the cost of living is rising, are concerned that their needs and interests are not being centered by the politicians and legislators that are supposed to represent them."

As electricity prices spike, more middle-income households are applying for government energy assistance despite their incomes being too high to qualify, Mark Wolfe, executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, told CBS News. The federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program is limited to people who earn less than 60% of their state's median income.

"People are dealing with high food bills, high gasoline bills, and they've just gone through high summer cooling bills," he said. "If you're living on a tight budget, from paycheck to paycheck, then the cost of driving goes up by $100, $150 a month, that might be the whole surplus in your budget."
Consumers "feel the government's not standing behind them, and they can't control these prices," Wolfe added.
Help decoding your energy bill

Consumer Reports said it's launching a new initiative called Power Smarter to help households reduce their energy costs. The effort includes a service called the CR Bill Decoder, where consumers can submit their electric bills. Consumer Reports, which will anonymize the bill data, will use the information to analyze trends and map prices across the U.S.

Bill Decoder "is intended to be a simple first step for anybody who wants to learn more about their energy bill and how they can take more power over their bill," Enright said. "We anonymize it and aggregate the data that we collect from it, and we'll be doing national-level and state-level evaluations of what's driving energy costs, and using that information to advocate for the American consumer to keep energy costs affordable."

title: Ohio race takes ugly turn with Ramaswamy ad featuring Acton's mom
summary: Democrat Amy Acton's estranged mother calls her a liar in a new Ramaswamy campaign ad. Acton's brother says the ad marks a "despicable low" and says their stepfather sexually abused Acton when she was a child.
story: A new attack ad from Republican Vivek Ramaswamy features the estranged mother of his opponent in the Ohio governor's race, Amy Acton, calling her a "liar." Acton's campaign and her brother denounced the ad as a "despicable low."

Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, whose husband was accused of raping Acton when she was a child, says in the spot, "It's not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy was a serious problem. She is a liar; she lies about her past."

Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, lashed out at Ramaswamy in response: "It's not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point."
He said that after their stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged, he and Acton were removed from the Arthurs' custody and lived with their father.

"Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."

The origin of the ad, which circulated on social media Monday night, was initially unclear because it lacked the mandatory disclosure of who paid for and authorized the spot. But on Tuesday, Ramaswamy told reporters it was "an ad from our campaign," according to The Columbus Dispatch. He defended the content of the ad, saying: "Every person who appears to know her the best … have told voters not to vote for her but to vote for me instead."

Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy, said in a statement earlier Tuesday, "We don't know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor."
The state Republican Party has not responded to a request for comment.

Vice President JD Vance, who represented Ohio in the Senate before becoming vice president, said Wednesday that "whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern" and that he was "a little bit disgusted" by fellow Republicans who are "whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America."

"Politics is a tough business," Vance said. "And my message to my fellow elected Republicans is, if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days."

Acton, who served as the state's public health commissioner under GOP Gov. Mike DeWine during the pandemic, has previously talked about being abused by her now-deceased stepfather. According to court records provided by the campaign, in 1978, Arthur was charged with raping Acton, when she was between 10 and 12 years old. He entered a not guilty plea.
Acton has also detailed struggles throughout her early childhood with poverty and homelessness, and records provided by her campaign show that the family lived in a tent for a year.
Acton told the Youngstown Vindicator in 2019 that once she and her brother were able to go live with their father, their lives became more stable.

"In the courthouse after they were charged, I went to give her a kiss, and she just turned her cheek away," Acton told The Vindicator seven years ago. "That was the last time I ever saw her." Her campaign says that court date remains the last time Acton saw her mother.

Her mother and her stepfather, released on bond, left Ohio without facing charges, the news site said. Warrants were issued for Cledith Arthur's arrest at least twice in the next few years, according to court records. Donna and Cledith Arthur lived in Pennsylvania until Cledith's death in 2004.
Ramaswamy's backers have launched other personal attacks against Acton, who has been leading in polls over the last month.
Other aspects of Acton's personal life have also resurfaced during the election, including an incident when police were called to her home in 2019 during what was characterized as a domestic dispute.
